asBirthCard.p: This card didn't come from your Sun, Moon or Rising. It came from the date. Add up every digit of your birthday, add the digits of the total again if it's over 22, and you get twenty, which is Judgement. Twenty is two tens, a full count gone through a second time, and that second pass is most of what the card is about. It comes after The Sun, where everything's in plain view, and just before The World, the last of the Majors, so it's the look back before the finish. Judgement's planet is Pluto. Pluto rules Scorpio and is in detriment in Taurus, meaning it works badly in the sign that most wants things left where they are, and it's the planet of what was buried coming back up. Look at the people in the picture standing up in their coffins, arms out, as the trumpet goes. Nearly everyone I've met with this birth card can name two or three times their life felt a bit like that.

The past doesn't stay filed away for you. You're the one at the school reunion who remembers exactly who said what on the bus in Year Nine, and it still bothers you a bit. Clearing out one cupboard turns into three evenings of old letters and a long think about a friendship you let go. You scroll back through a message thread from years ago, just to check what really happened, and come away seeing it differently. Every so often you go through a quiet patch where something you've been doing for years starts to feel wrong, and then it's over, you've resigned or moved or said the thing, and people are surprised because they never saw it coming. You'd seen it coming for the best part of eighteen months and just hadn't mentioned it to anyone.

You let other people change. Most people are worse at that than they'd admit, and hold everyone to the version they first met, the flaky flatmate, the brother who was a mess at twenty, the colleague who got it badly wrong on their first project. You don't. When a friend comes back sober after two hard years, or an old enemy from work turns out to have grown up, you give them the new version straight away and you mean it. Having been through a few endings and restarts of your own, you know they're real. You're also good at finishing things properly. The last conversation before a breakup, the handover when you leave a job, the eulogy nobody else wanted to write. You do it cleanly, and people remember it was you who did.

The fresh start can turn into a habit. When something gets hard, part of you reaches for the clean slate, a new city, a new job, deleting the account and starting over, when what the situation actually needed was a patient fix. Patching things up bores you, to be honest, and a year of slow repair feels like it'll never end. You also keep a record of people. You'd never call it that, but you remember the time your friend didn't turn up for you in 2019, and some part of you is still deciding whether they've been forgiven. At a family Christmas you can feel yourself sorting the room into who's done the work and who hasn't. That's the Pluto in this card, which can keep a thing below ground for years, and the people you're quietly assessing usually have no idea.

A loss sends you backwards first. A job goes, or someone dies, or a friend stops returning your calls, and you go back over all of it, what you missed, where it started, what you should have seen, and a whole weekend can disappear into that. About a week later the going-over produces a verdict, and then you want to act on it fast. You draft the resignation at two in the morning, or decide a relationship's finished, or cut off someone who was only half to blame. The people around you find this hard. Some feel judged and some feel dropped, because you've shut a door they didn't know was even being discussed. What helps is a plain rule that nothing irreversible happens for a fortnight, and a phone call to someone who knew you three versions ago.

You need a partner who can handle you changing. Somewhere in any long relationship you tend to come up from one of your quiet patches wanting to talk about who the two of you are now, and a partner who wanted things to stay exactly as they were on the first date usually finds that unsettling. Pick someone who's curious about it. You also go back over old relationships long after they're done, sometimes with the ex, which can confuse whoever you're with. Tell them what it is. It's usually you finishing the thinking you didn't get to do at the time. The less obvious need is being forgiven. You're so used to handing out second chances that you don't expect to get one, and the first time a partner lets a real mistake go without bringing it up again, it can floor you.

A job that's merely fine gets harder for you every year, until one day you can't face it at all. The work you stay in has to matter, even in a small way. You're good at anything that means looking back honestly and deciding what comes next, the post-mortem on a failed project, the audit, the restructure nobody else will lead, family history, counselling, careers advice for people starting over at forty. You're also often the one who calls time at work, on the project that's been limping along for two years, and people are relieved once somebody's said it. Career changes are common with this card, and they often come late. Keep a second skill ticking over on the side, a short course or a bit of freelance, so that if you do make the jump you aren't starting from nothing.

In your twenties the exits tend to be dramatic. You try on a few lives and change course a lot, and when you leave something it's usually with a slammed door or a whole friendship group left behind. By the mid-thirties there's often been one real reckoning, a marriage ended or begun, one career dropped for another, a move home or away from it for good. People with this card usually say that was the decade they started noticing a change coming earlier, while it was still quiet enough to plan for. The fifties tend to bring the long review. Parents age or die, old family stories come out, and people from twenty years ago get back in touch. A lot of Judgement people end up as the one in the family who knows the history, and younger relatives come to them when their own lives turn over.

Next time you catch yourself replaying an old mistake, in the shower, on the drive home, at three in the morning, stop and say out loud roughly when it happened, the month and the year. Then say one thing you've done differently since. Only one, and it can be small. You're giving the past a date so it stops acting like it happened this morning. Do it every time the replay starts, for a month.
